newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Ogata gets heroine's welcome at Zaire refugee camp.
newsitem.headline: Ogata gets heroine's welcome at Zaire refugee camp.

text.p: UN refugee chief Sadako Ogata received a heroine's welcome when she visited Rwandan refugees on Saturday in the village of Tingi-Tingi on the edge of the combat zone of Zaire's civil war.
An estimated 120,000 Rwandan Hutus have been trapped by the war in Tingi -Tingi after fleeing west from earlier fighting along the border with Rwanda and Burundi.
More have been arriving in the past 24 hours after the nearby town of Amisi fell to Tutsi-led rebels in eastern Zaire.
Ogata shook hands with skinny, malnourished children. Heavily guarded by Zairean soldiers, she visited the medical centre and a warehouse where food supplies are stocked.
Living conditions have improved slightly since mid-December when the first groups of refugees flocked to Tingi-Tingi.
Aid agencies have organised food distribution but many refugees complain about the quantity and quality of the food.

"Up to 30 deaths are reported here daily. It's difficult to confirm that the worst has been avoided but we have to acknowledge that an effort has been made to raise the health standards of the refugees here," Doctor Laurent Bedel of Medecins du Monde told Reuters.
He said there had been an outbreak of cholera but it had been quickly contained.
"It was not an epidemic as such," Bedel said, adding that water purification equipment had been in place for some time.
"I am surprised by the strength of the people who walked for months (to Tingi-Tingi)," Ogata told a news conference.
"Our immediate task is to get the health situation to a certain level," she said.
She raised concerns about the fast-moving front line which is a major threat to the refugees as the rebels have advanced to Amisi, 70 km (45 miles) south of Tingi-Tingi.
"I am appealing to those who have information about the front line. I will see the governor and know what the impending danger is. It's a huge concentration of people," she said.
However, she added it was up to Zaire to prevent attacks on refugees on its soil.
Innocent Seruntanga, who coordinates administrative matters here, said that panic was sweeping across Tingi-Tingi as the rebels captured more towns.

"Hunger will certainly force some refugees to go back to Rwanda but only a tiny minority may be willing to return home, " he said, adding that the vast majority would stay in Zaire despite the rebels' advance.
Ogata pointed out that Zaire and the UN refugee agency had reached an agreement on repatriating the refugees.
"The refugees have to move out. They have to go home but it it not clear how, when and under what conditions," she said.
The rebels, who are seeking to topple Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, have seized a portion of Zairean territory along its border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
The demoralised Zairean army last month launched a much-trumpeted counter-offensive.
